machatzit-hashekel/4:ב: And furthermore Tosafot in Avodah Zarah are stringent, etc. — meaning, regarding chametz; and see Shach siman 108 note 13. And thereby Maharil's proof is rejected; and Maharil siman 186: it seems you were uncertain, since chametz is in any amount, whether reicha is significant, etc., and it appears there is no distinction according to Levi who permits — proof that Levi permits slaughtered meat roasted with nevelah meat in every case, even when both are the same species, even according to Levi who holds min b'mino in any amount; and similarly proven there in perek Kol Tzvi, which challenges according to Levi due to mixture of flavors: what difference to me kid and kid, and what difference kid and lamb — let us say there is no difference kid and kid, for it is min b'mino; and R' Yehudah and Rabbi, etc., min b'mino in any amount, but even kid and lamb which is min b'she'eino mino; and Rav also holds min b'mino in any amount — end of Maharil's words. His intent: we say in perek Kol Tzvi daf 76 — it was stated: slaughtered meat that is lean roasted with nevelah meat — Rav said forbidden, for what reason? Reicha is significant; Levi said permitted, reicha is not significant. They challenged: one may not roast two Paschal lambs as one due to mixture — is it not mixture of flavors? And it is difficult for Levi — not due to mixture of bodies (and the reason for mixture of bodies or flavors is that thereby the Pesach is eaten not according to its count) — the Gemara answers from the end teaching even kid and lamb; if not due to bodies, meaning the teaching says even kid and lamb; if not mixture of flavors, what difference kid and lamb from kid and kid? Rather what — mixture of flavors, and permitted; let it be a refutation of Rav — end of Gemara. Maharil infers from the challengers' challenge to Rav: why even kid and lamb — what is the novelty in kid and lamb more than kid and kid? If not due to mixture of flavors; and one may say that even according to us who rule like Levi, nevertheless regarding chametz reicha is significant, for Levi concedes that a minute amount exists. Rather Rav holds reicha is a complete flavor — if so, kid and lamb is properly a novelty, unlike kid and kid which is min b'mino, and the baraita follows R' Yehudah who holds min b'mino in any amount — if so, forbidden even according to Levi who says reicha is not significant, for a minute amount exists; but even kid and lamb which is min b'she'eino mino is forbidden because it is a complete flavor; rather perforce one must say the Gemara holds according to Levi reicha is not a complete flavor, and if not significant, even a minute amount of flavor does not exist; and if so, it properly challenges what difference kid, etc.; and so Magen Avraham wrote that according to Rif his proof is rejected, for it appears one may say on Maharil's proof that even if Levi concedes a minute amount exists, nevertheless it properly challenges what difference kid, etc., although kid and kid is min b'mino; nevertheless the baraita speaks l'chatchila, for it teaches one may not roast; and regarding l'chatchila there is no distinction between min and she'eino mino, for whatever forbids in min b'dieved due to forbidding in any amount in she'eino mino is in any case forbidden l'chatchila, for we rule one may not nullify a prohibition l'chatchila; and one must say it is difficult for Maharil — for Tosafot there explain Rashi that Levi argues only b'dieved but l'chatchila concedes it is forbidden; if so, why does the Gemara challenge Levi from the baraita one may not roast two Paschal lambs — the baraita speaks l'chatchila, perforce Levi permits even l'chatchila, and it is difficult for Maharil according to the questioner who holds Levi concedes a minute amount exists; and therefore regarding chametz reicha is significant — if so, it is itself difficult why Levi permits l'chatchila, for one may not nullify a prohibition l'chatchila; and if so, it does not challenge Levi at all from the baraita one may not roast two Paschal lambs; and perforce one must say the Gemara holds this is not called nullifying a prohibition since one does not intend to nullify, as below siman 453 seif 3; and see Taz and Yoreh De'ah siman 84 note 45 in Shach and in many places; and therefore Maharil's proof stands, for certainly a minute amount exists — properly kid and lamb is a novelty as she'eino mino, and one would think reicha is only a minute amount and even l'chatchila in she'eino mino is permitted since one does not intend to nullify — we learn that it is a complete flavor; and this suffices to reject the questioner's view of Maharil, who holds Rav considers reicha a complete flavor and Levi who we rule like him at least holds a minute amount of flavor exists. But according to Rif, Rav himself has only a minute amount of flavor — if so, certainly for Levi even a minute amount does not exist, for otherwise why does Levi disagree — because Levi holds min b'mino is nullified? Then their dispute does not depend on reicha at all, but whether min b'mino is in any amount or not, and they should dispute in general regarding min b'mino; perforce Levi holds that even according to those who hold min b'mino in any amount, nevertheless reicha is not significant, for a minute amount of flavor does not exist; rather Rif holds we rule like Rav over Levi for reasons Rif wrote there, except one cannot rule like Rav since Rav concedes there is only a minute amount of flavor. Rather Rav follows his reason of min b'mino in any amount, and slaughtered meat with nevelah is min b'mino. And if so, according to us who rule min b'mino is nullified, one cannot rule like Rav here; if so, regarding chametz which we rule forbids in any amount, we rule like Rav that reicha is significant. And therefore Maharil's proof is rejected; perforce according to Rif, that which the Gemara challenges Rav why even kid and lamb — it should have said only that the reason is mixture of flavors — if so, why is kid and lamb which is min b'she'eino mino forbidden, since even for Rav reicha is only a minute amount; perforce, since the baraita speaks regarding l'chatchila, as it teaches one may not roast, etc., and regarding l'chatchila for Rav even she'eino mino is forbidden, for one may not nullify a prohibition l'chatchila — perforce one must say this is called intent to nullify; nevertheless it properly challenges Levi, for perforce Levi permits even l'chatchila, for perforce Levi holds even a minute amount of flavor does not exist, as above. And therefore Maharil's proof stands, for it properly challenges what difference kid, etc.; for although this is min b'mino and that she'eino mino, nevertheless since the baraita speaks l'chatchila, and regarding l'chatchila there is no distinction between min and she'eino mino, for one may not nullify a prohibition l'chatchila, as above:
mishnah-berurah/5:ע: (54) And b'dieved one need not be stringent — meaning, all the matters in the gloss where custom is to be stringent apply only l'chatchila; but b'dieved, if they already cooked them even without rinsing and soaking and cannot keep them until after Pesach, one should not cast them to loss, and it is permitted to eat them on Pesach; and all the more their mixture is not forbidden even in less than sixty, since it is only a rabbinic doubt of a minute amount. And if there is garlic or other davar charif in butcher goods, they forbid mixtures on Pesach like full chametz in any amount, since it was cut with a chametz knife; and even if the knife was wiped clean and is not ben yomo, it is still forbidden. Some permit mixtures from butcher goods in less than sixty in great financial loss if the knife was wiped and is not ben yomo. This applies only to garlic and onion in the brine; but garlic that they chop very fine and mix into salt with which they salt meat to dry it, so that the garlic aroma spreads into the meat — it is permitted to eat the meat on Pesach through soaking and rinsing like other dry meat; and specifically if they rinsed before Pesach, but during Pesach rinsing does not help, only peeling [Eshel Avraham]:
mishnah-berurah/6:א: (78) That they placed in the mortar — and even if it is ben yomo on the day they pounded in it, provided it is now clean; and even if salt has been placed there for twenty-four hours, pickling applies only to a moist item and not to a dry one:
mishnah-berurah/7:א: (81) Unripe grapes that were pounded before Pesach, etc. — Mishna Berurah holds that unripe grapes are not considered davar charif; but according to what we rule in Yoreh De'ah siman 96 that even sour fruits are included in davar charif — unripe grapes are also included; and therefore through charif and pressure, chametz from the mortar is absorbed in the unripe grapes, and there are not sixty in the unripe grapes against the entire mortar to nullify it — therefore even before Pesach one should be stringent. See Acharonim who wrote that in a case of pressing need one may rely on Poskim who hold sour fruits are not davar charif. And know that even without pressing need, our stringency regarding the mortar applies specifically to a mortar customarily used for chametz; but in our mortars whose primary use is spices and aromatics, there is only concern for a minute amount of taste that is nullified in sixty before Pesach, even in a ben yomo vessel:
mishnah-berurah/7:ה: (85) During Pesach — and before Pesach the unripe grapes are permitted through rinsing; but during Pesach, since it forbids in any amount, one should be stringent l'chatchila not to eat them. See Magen Avraham, whose view is that one need not be stringent even on Pesach except for things regularly done by gentiles, such as buying fish they cut with their chametz knives; but if done incidentally in a Jew's home, such as cutting with a chametz knife a non-charif item on Pesach — rinsing or scraping suffices:
mishnah-berurah/7:ו: (86) To chametz adhering to it — all this if he cut with it a non-charif item; but with a davar charif [and likewise unripe grapes, according to us who hold it is davar charif], even if the knife was certainly clean and he cut with it before Pesach, it is forbidden to eat on Pesach. However, this applies specifically to a knife they are accustomed to sometimes use hot with chametz and chametz is absorbed in it; but if they never use it hot, such as an onion cut with the knife with which they scrape dough from the kneading trough, and it was clean — the onion is permitted, even if cut on Pesach, since that knife was never used hot and cold does not absorb and discharge:
mishnah-berurah/8:ג: (91) According to all — and behold, according to what is explained below in seif 9 in the gloss, that we are stringent regarding noten ta'am lifgam on Pesach, one may not permit unless they removed the chametz from the vessel before erev night b'eyna:
mishnah-berurah/9:א: (92) Dry in dry — meaning, a slice of chametz became mixed among matzah slices and is not recognizable; but if a loaf became mixed among loaves, according to all it is not nullified, for it is a davar shebeminyan and is not nullified even in a thousand, as explained in Yoreh De'ah siman 110:
mishnah-berurah/9:ב: (93) Not nullified — since if moist became mixed its prohibition is in any amount, they were also stringent regarding it when dry. And therefore specifically when mixed during Pesach; but if mixed on erev Pesach until night, we hold above in seif 2 that its law is like other prohibitions — and therefore moist is nullified in noten ta'am like other prohibitions, and likewise dry is like other prohibitions and nullified by majority. Nevertheless, they must all be eaten before night, for otherwise we say it returns and revives on Pesach, as proven above in seif 4 in the gloss. Some wrote that according to the first view, dry in dry is not nullified specifically when the prohibition is from the chametz itself; but if the permitted item itself only absorbed a minute amount of chametz, such as matzah in which a leavened wheat kernel was baked and afterward became mixed with others — it is nullified one in two even during Pesach; but many Acharonim disagree. Acharonim also wrote that a chametz vessel mixed with Pesach vessels on Pesach — its law is like dry in dry, not nullified, forbidden to use on Pesach; and even if mixed on erev Pesach one should be stringent not to use them; however, if the chametz vessel was not ben yomo, in a place where Yom Tov joy would be prevented, one may be lenient if mixed on erev Pesach:
mishnah-berurah/9:ג: (94) And some say chametz on Pesach, etc. — their reason: specifically in a moist mixture, where in other prohibitions the measure is noten ta'am, the Sages were stringent regarding chametz that it is in any amount; but in a dry item, where in other prohibitions one in two nullifies, likewise chametz on Pesach:
mishnah-berurah/10:א: (96) Noten ta'am lifgam is permitted, etc. — the reason: although the Sages were stringent to forbid chametz on Pesach in any amount, since although a minute amount is present there is nevertheless prohibition upon it; but when the taste is spoiled, its prohibition is entirely nullified and it cannot forbid mixtures even for consumption, even if there are not sixty against it; and its law on Pesach is like all the particulars explained in Yoreh De'ah siman 103 regarding other prohibitions [see there]. All this regarding mixtures; but regarding the chametz itself, see above siman 442 seif 9 in Mishna Berurah:
mishnah-berurah/10:ה: (100) Forbidden — nevertheless regarding benefit, to sell to a gentile one may be lenient in this since it is also only a minute amount. See Peri Megadim note 11, who leans that on the last Yom Tov one may be lenient if both happen together, even for consumption:
mishnah-berurah/11:ב: (102) That became mixed before Pesach, etc., nullified in sixty — meaning, if it became mixed before Pesach in sixty, it is permitted after Pesach [even according to those who forbid because it returns and revives on Pesach; if it remained until after Pesach it is permitted according to all, even for consumption]. And if it became mixed in less than sixty and Pesach passed — forbidden. The author follows his view stated at the beginning of siman 442, that one transgresses bal yeira'eh on a mixture of chametz kezayit even if there is not a kezayit in k'dei achilat pras, provided there are not sixty to nullify it — and this is specifically min b'she'eino mino; but in min b'mino, which the Torah nullifies by majority, even if one in two became mixed and Pesach passed, it is permitted for consumption [Magen Avraham]. Eshel Avraham at end of this seif: forbidden for consumption but permitted for benefit according to all. Acharonim wrote: forbidden to mix chametz l'chatchila before Pesach in sixty in order to eat on Pesach; but permitted to mix in sixty in order to keep until after Pesach:
mishnah-berurah/11:ה: (105) Nullified in sixty — all this when moist in moist or dry in moist, whose measure is generally noten ta'am; but if dry became mixed in dry in all the cases the author described, even one in two nullifies and is permitted after Pesach for consumption. And know that the last case the author described — mixed after Pesach and requiring sixty — is according to Tur; but many Poskim disagree and hold that when mixed after Pesach, whether min b'mino or she'eino mino, majority suffices, for they did not penalize to forbid when mixed after Pesach if the permitted portion is greater; Acharonim wrote that in great financial loss or pressing need one may rely to be lenient:
mishnah-berurah/11:ו: (106) Redemption suffices, etc. — and through this it is permitted even for consumption; and specifically in the third case the author described — mixed after Pesach; but if mixed before Pesach, and all the more during Pesach when one transgressed bal yeira'eh on the mixture — it is not permitted after Pesach through redemption, only for benefit and not consumption, for one tastes chametz pieces. Dough that leavened in beer yeast that passed Pesach — although there are sixty against the yeast, it is forbidden even for benefit, for yeast is a davar ham'amid and is not nullified even in a thousand, and is as if entirely prohibited; nevertheless in great financial loss one may permit it for benefit by casting the benefit of the prohibition to the Dead Sea, and one may sell it to a gentile and receive only the value of the dough without the yeast. Permitted to put wheat starch or animal milk into wine when there is present against it to clarify it; we are not concerned lest one eat it with meat or on Pesach, for even if one forgets and eats, there is no prohibition since it is already nullified, and this is not nullifying a prohibition l'chatchila since the intent is only to fix the wine:
mishnah-berurah/12:ב: (108) Lest it fall into the food — and b'dieved, if it fell and there are sixty against it, there are differing views among Acharonim whether it forbids in any amount; see above in Mishna Berurah note 14; and to keep it until after Pesach is permitted according to all:
turei-zahav/1:א: In any amount. Rambam gave the reason that chametz is a davar sheyesh lo matirin; Rosh at the end of Avodah Zarah gave the reason that people do not avoid chametz all year, therefore they were stringent regarding it in any amount. See seif 2 that on the last Yom Tov it is permitted to keep it:
turei-zahav/1:ג: And specifically where, etc. Meaning, e.g., when the oven is small and does not hold twelve esronim and is sealed, and chametz and matzah are both uncovered inside the oven — in this we permit b'dieved in other prohibitions, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 108; but in matzah it is forbidden in this. But if the oven is large, even if sealed, or one of the dishes is covered — whether chametz or matzah — it is permitted, for reicha does not apply at all. And in Yoreh De'ah there Rama ruled that in financial loss one may rely on the lenient Poskim, and it is like other prohibitions; and Poskim wrote in the name of Rabbenu Tam that in bread reicha does not apply at all — therefore bread chametz baked with matzah bread does not forbid, although these three matters apply status: and similarly Shulchan Aruch brought in siman 461 seif 5:
turei-zahav/4:א: That it is moist in moist. It appears to me that if moist became mixed in moist in less than sixty before Pesach, one may increase upon it before Pesach until there are sixty so it will be permitted on Pesach, and this is not [called] nullifying a prohibition l'chatchila; and I wrote proof in Hilchot Sukkah siman 626 seif 1 [see there]. And this moist in moist does not exclude flour in flour, which also mixes well, as Beit Yosef wrote in the name of Semag; see siman 453 seif 3; and similarly ruled in Shulchan Aruch below siman 451 seif 27 regarding a spit — we do not say it returns and revives:
turei-zahav/5:א: Permitted. The reason is that the concern for leavening in salt that was salted is nullified in sixty before Pesach and does not return and revive; and if so, the author did not need to write it is permitted, since above he wrote there are those who disagree and hold it returns and revives — it appears the Shulchan Aruch ruled like the lenient view, for here there were two leniencies: perhaps there was no chametz in the salt at all; and if there was, say it was nullified before Pesach according to the lenient view; and those who disagree whom Rama brought is R' Yitzchak Gaon whom Tur brought — who forbids cheese milked by an Israelite before Pesach if not known they were careful about leavening, because R' Yitzchak Gaon holds chametz returns and revives on Pesach; and if so, why did Rama write the custom is to be stringent, since in seif 4 he wrote the custom follows the first view? One must explain the opposite: the reason for the custom to be stringent here is that the salt is visible on these items, and perhaps there is chametz visible among the salt, therefore rinsing does not help:
turei-zahav/5:ב: And there are those who disagree. Siman 497 seif 13 proves the Shulchan Aruch rules like the first view [see there]; and similarly siman 451 note 27 regarding a spit:
turei-zahav/5:ג: Three times before Pesach. Meaning, in a vessel that is not chametz l'chatchila; b'dieved it helps even in a chametz vessel, for cold does not discharge — and Rama mentioned only meat; and it appears the same law applies to fish, that they may be permitted through rinsing like meat, except I have not seen practice to permit fish through rinsing. One may give a reason: Semag wrote — however people are accustomed not to eat aged cheese or salted fish, perhaps because they are accustomed to eat them without rinsing; but salted meat requires rinsing — end of his words; it appears this is because since people are accustomed to eat fish without rinsing, there is concern they will eat them without rinsing, unlike meat. Nevertheless, once there was a shortage of meat and I permitted rinsing fish for Pesach, for it appears to me they did not forbid fish except those salted recently, unlike fish salted in barrels that cannot be without rinsing — this is preferable to meat; but cheese plainly rinsing does not help and is like korkshita. Moharach wrote in siman 451 that if meat was given after they kashered it in a vessel used with chametz for twenty-four hours, the meat is forbidden for Pesach, for it is like pickled like cooked; and I wrote in Yoreh De'ah siman 105 that one may not forbid because of pickled like cooked in a prohibited vessel, for it is lifgam after the twenty-four-hour period which is pickling time, and lifgam is permitted before Pesach; and it appears to me dry meat hanging in a room where flour is managed is chametz b'eyna and rinsing does not help:
turei-zahav/5:ד: But in fat from rendering. Beit Yosef challenged: behold we rule stam vessels are not ben yomo, and he elaborated; and it appears to me that here we do not say so, for I already wrote in Yoreh De'ah siman 122 in the name of Darkei Moshe in the name of Hagahot Maimoniyot that an Israelite has remedy through asking, and if he does not know he is penalized; and it appears there is no penalty except for that Israelite whose pot it is, who should have known and did not; but not for another — end of Darkei Moshe. And it appears that although this view is not agreed for halacha as Shulchan Aruch wrote in seif 8, nevertheless for Pesach all hold thus, for every person is accustomed to be careful in everything needed for Pesach when preparing to guard from leavening; therefore one who rendered fat in every cooked item should have been careful that the pan is certainly not ben yomo — therefore he is penalized to forbid his cooked food from eating on Pesach, as above — this is correct. And it appears that in preserves, which are sharp and acidic, this is forbidden even in other prohibitions even if not ben yomo; therefore one should be stringent even on the last Yom Tov:
turei-zahav/5:ו: Within two months. In Terumat HaDeshen and Piskei Mahari siman 149 this law is in the name of Semag within thirty days; and so appears primary, for we find thirty as the measure in other Pesach matters; and Rama himself copied in siman 442 seif 3 regarding paper adhesion — and they have one reason together with this here:
turei-zahav/7:_: Unripe grapes that are pounded, etc. Semak wrote that it is cold and has no power to discharge; and even if it discharges a minute amount, it is nullified before Pesach immediately, similar to onions cut with a milking knife and placed with meat, as Rabbenu Yerucham explained — end of his words; and his explanation is what we say in Yoreh De'ah siman 96 that with davar charif and pressure of the knife there is prohibition, as there seif 1; therefore he said here even if it discharges — through mortar pressure and there is davar charif, for unripe grapes have acidity; nevertheless one need not nullify it, for the discharge alone [does not make all forbidden], unlike onions cut with a milking knife placed with meat, where not all the onion becomes forbidden but we measure against what was absorbed in them, unlike cutting with a forbidden knife where all the onion becomes nevelah; here too, since done before Pesach when it was still permitted, afterward on Pesach it is permitted since the minor discharge was already nullified; therefore if done on Pesach it is certainly forbidden if cut with a chametz knife. Chametz — even if the knife is clean, because of knife pressure and it is davar charif, as in Yoreh De'ah regarding radish siman 96 where some forbid even in cold — therefore it is difficult why Rama wrote stam knife is not presumed clean; for it appears even if certainly clean one must forbid if cut on Pesach with a chametz knife:
turei-zahav/8:_: Olives for which they were careful, etc. Tur wrote: olives pickled all year — according to Beit HaTov who forbids radish and onion with an old forbidden knife, comparing them to a wheat kernel, etc., for in the entire knife we measure — and therefore all the olives became chametz, etc. It is difficult: why do we not measure sixty against the knife, for certainly all the olives have sixty against it, as in Yoreh De'ah siman 96 regarding onions seif 2; for here too when the olives absorbed from the knife it was still permitted; and do not challenge the old knife of siman 96, for Tur at the end wrote: and it appears to me that even according to Beit HaTov, if they were careful to cut with a new knife, etc. — implying without care in the knife there is no leniency through nullification like the knife size; and it appears this cutting of olives speaks before they were pickled, when they are still sharp; or Tur wrote that through water at pickling their sharpness is nullified. And in Or Zaru'a Orach Chayim general rule 38 he wrote: and moreover regarding chametz prohibition, olives cut with a chametz knife do not forbid b'eyna except if cut after pickling; but if cut before pickling, he permits eating them on Pesach — not found so in our Tur, rather the opposite as above; perhaps he brought from a different Orchos Chaim, therefore it works here that sixty does not help to nullify whether all sixty against the knife, since each takes individually before pickling and there is not sixty in each individually against the knife — it stands in what it received and combination does not help, for there is nothing to combine them and carry taste from one to the other, unlike there with onions where cooking gravy carries from one to another; but here in pickling each is pickled individually through placing in water — therefore combination does not help. And do not challenge unripe grapes mentioned in the previous seif, that there the combination helps to nullify mortar discharge, as below, for there all were pounded and mixed well together as they received together — therefore combination helps to nullify discharge, as above — correct. And that which is written here to permit even if they were not careful to pickle in a new pot is because Tur wrote their sharpness is nullified at pickling time since water is placed on them — and one should not say afterward they become sharp again; rather one should be careful about inserting the knife for the reason we mentioned. In Tur: and so it appears, etc. — it is difficult how he brings proof from what was cut on Pesach itself to what was written above about olives of the whole year; one may say he brings proof only that olives' law is equal because of sharpness to a wheat kernel mentioned in the Gemara; for onion is also similar to a wheat kernel and Rosh forbids if cut with stam knife even though lifgam, as Tur wrote in his name; rather certainly forbidden because it is davar charif:
turei-zahav/9:א: Even in a thousand not nullified. Beit Yosef wrote: its reason appears because of davar sheyesh lo matirin, or he holds dry in dry is nullified one in two in a prohibition dependent on noten ta'am; but where they were more stringent than noten ta'am, there is no difference between dry and moist, as Mordechai wrote in perek Kol Sha'ah — end of his words; and therefore if mixed before Pesach one in two in dry, when then its measure is noten ta'am, its law is like other prohibitions:
turei-zahav/9:ב: And some say chametz is equal, etc. Automatically, if the chametz is a piece fit for honor or other things not nullified in other prohibitions, plainly so on Pesach too; except in Rashi whom Beit Yosef brings, who distinguishes according to R' Akiva between a whole loaf and a slice of loaf; Beit Yosef wrote we do not rule like R' Akiva — therefore we do not distinguish here, for R' Akiva's reason is that a loaf is important in itself, and we hold a matter fit for honor depends on context:
turei-zahav/11:ב: And in less than sixty, redemption suffices, etc. Meaning, moist in moist requires sixty; nevertheless here, since Pesach passed, the prohibition is only a penalty for transgressing bal yeira'eh; and since he cast benefit to the Dead Sea, there is no penalty and therefore permitted even for consumption, according to Beit Yosef and not like Hagahot Maimoniyot who permits only benefit in this and in dry in dry plainly one in two suffices — forbidden even without casting benefit to the Dead Sea, for here one did not transgress bal yeira'eh since the Torah nullifies one in two; and even rabbinically the prohibition is only from the stringency of any amount, and we do not penalize except even one in one permitted at least through redemption. And in Hagahot Maimoniyot on this law he wrote: if leavened wheat kernels became mixed in permitted wheat and not known until after Pesach, etc., as Beit Yosef — one may not learn from this that if known before Pesach redemption after Pesach does not suffice; this is not R' Shimon's reason of penalty after Pesach without distinction whether transgressed intentionally or unintentionally — in both we penalize; and just as if mixed after Pesach unintentionally in sixty it is permitted even if intentional on Pesach, as Rashi, Rosh, and Tur wrote explicitly in this siman — so too redemption helps even if intentional. And furthermore, what depends on knowing? For in any case the mixture is unintentional; they simply did not mention there incidentally, for certainly we are not dealing with a wicked person who knew and did not burn at the time of prohibition. And above in this siman seif 3 I wrote that even l'chatchila one may increase on mixtures before Pesach since still permitted; and proof from Sukkah — if so here in dry in dry if one in two, one may add permitted wheat and grind, and its law is like moist in moist above seif 3, and one may eat even on Pesach; and if he wishes to keep after Pesach he need not do this and it is permitted even without redemption to the Dead Sea — all this appears correct to me; and although Moharach wrote some particulars here not as I wrote, nevertheless after investigation the matters are clear:
turei-zahav/12:_: Lest it fall, etc. And if kartin fell into food, the food is forbidden, as above regarding chametz nokshah such as tarika and the like in siman 442; but permitted to keep and after Pesach as above. Tur brought above in this siman and likewise Ba'al HaItur: specifically chametz b'eyna; but discharge from the walls of a vessel regarding honey and oil of a gentile on Pesach, etc., is nullified; and for several days our master practiced prohibition, and the stringent 572 — end of his words. It is difficult: how is it nullified, behold sixty is required, and what is inside the vessel is not sixty against the entire vessel, as Beit Yosef wrote; it appears Ba'al HaItur follows his reason that also in Yoreh De'ah siman 93 he holds there is sixty against vessel discharge, as Beit Yosef there according to him; and although Tur does not hold this view, he brought his words because some mention what Ba'al HaItur wrote, such as meat not careful in salting; and furthermore perhaps he holds as Mordechai Kol Sha'ah in the name of Or Zarua to permit a beer barrel — rinse with water, wipe, and put wine and honey for Pesach, because beer taste is nullified in sixty before Pesach and we do not measure against the entire vessel since the permitted absorbed — and Rama ruled thus in siman 451:
